Lithe

/LYTHE/ - rhymes with writhe · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Lithe means graceful, flexible, supple.

Otters are lithe enough to turn a full circle inside their own length.

Worked Example

In the tango final, the oldest couple on the floor won on lithe economy: no lunges, no strain, just long supple turns that seemed to have no corners at all.

Lithe says more than 'flexible' — it bundles bend and grace into one word. A gymnast's stretched hamstring is flexibility; movement that flows soft and effortless through every joint is lithe, and the word always compliments.

How Lithe Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

supple

supple: bends softly and easily — the flexibility without the grace

nimble

nimble: quick and light — speed more than bend

Antonyms

stiff

stiff: barely able to bend

ungainly

ungainly: awkward and graceless in motion

How Strong Is It? — limber → supple → lithe

limber vs. lithe

limber vs. lithe: Limber means loose enough to move and stretch — it stops well short of lithe.

supple vs. lithe

supple vs. lithe: Supple goes further than limber — it bends softly, without resistance — but stops short of lithe, which adds grace to the bending.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — lithe

Root — lithe: whole word from Old English lithe, gentle, soft, mild

Put it together

Put it together: Lithe is a single Old English root with nothing to peel off. A thousand years ago it meant gentle and mild — a lithe answer, a lithe breeze — and over centuries the softness moved into the body itself: what bends gently, without stiffness, is lithe.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Old English lithe left no everyday descendants — its one child, the fairy-tale word lithesome, is rarer than lithe itself. The root's whole career in modern English is this single supple adjective.

Strength Check

Word Choice

admiring

Lithe is for living bodies in motion — dancers, cats, willows — and it always admires. Choose supple when you mean pure soft bendability, nimble when you mean quickness, and lithe when flexibility moves with grace. It rarely fits objects or ideas: a lithe argument sounds as odd as a graceful doorknob.
